content.reading_plan: This is an 18-page research article in the International Journal of Energy Research, written in a dense, two-column technical style. It combines explanatory prose, numbered equations, system diagrams, numerical tables, performance plots, a conclusion, nomenclature, references, and three short mathematical appendices. I will follow its printed order, generally taking a few paragraphs at a time and slowing down around assumptions, equations, and changes in assessment method. Claims and supporting material will be recorded separately. Readings of visual elements will be paraphrased and identified by element number. Repeated claims will be identified as restatements rather than entered again, except where the later wording introduces a different numerical statement or qualification.

reading_path.location: Page 10453, title and Summary
reading_path.moves: Introduces the proposed system, states its motivation and operating scope, and previews the methods and principal findings.

claims.text: The waste heat management of the data center cooling systems has a significant share in the energy-efficient operations of the data centers.

The proposed hybrid uses waste heat from two-phase liquid-immersion data center cooling to heat the feed of a direct contact membrane distillation module. The cooling load is 0.7–1.5 kW and the membrane area is 5–75 cm².
Two-phase liquid-immersion cooling is promising because of its high heat flux removal performance, but research on its waste heat management remains insufficient.
The study assesses the hybrid thermodynamically, economically, and thermoeconomically, using a system-specific exergy-cost matrix.
The reported maximum thermal and exergy efficiencies are 64.5% and 53.7%, respectively; daily distilled water production reaches 6.13 kg at the highest cooling load and membrane area.
Although the hybrid has higher capital and operating costs than stand-alone cooling, its reported payback period of 3.72 years makes it economically feasible for real applications.
The hybrid's levelized product cost is reported as 2.69–5.33 SGD/h. The Summary places the optimization trade-off at 1.1 kW and a membrane area between 5.12 and 5.19 cm².

reading_path.meaning: The opening supplies a compressed account of the whole project. These are the authors' announced findings; the body has not yet supplied the model, assumptions, or calculations supporting them.

reading_path.location: Pages 10453–10454, Section 1, opening discussion of data center energy demand
reading_path.moves: Establishes the practical problem with demand figures, explains why cooling is necessary, and distinguishes two cooling families.

claims.text: Increasing demand for ICT makes uninterrupted data center operation increasingly important, while stable operation entails substantial energy consumption.
Global data center energy demand reached 200 TWh in 2018.

support.text: The authors cite Jones for this global demand figure.

citations.reference_entry: Jones N. The information factories. Nature. 2018;561:163-166. https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-018-06610-y.

claims.text: The cited projection puts United States data center energy consumption at 70 TWh in 2020.

support.text: The projection is attributed to Jin and Bai.

citations.reference_entry: Jin C, Bai X. The study of servers' arrangement and air distribution strategy under partial load in data centers. Sust Cities Soc. 2019;49:101617. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scs.2019.101617.

claims.text: ICT equipment can demand up to 100 times the energy of standard office facilities.

support.text: The authors support this comparison with the review by Oro and colleagues.

citations.reference_entry: Oro E, Depoorter V, Garcia A, Salom J. Energy efficiency and renewable energy integration in data centres. Strategies and modeling review. Renew Sust Energ Rev. 2015;42:429-445. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2014.10.035.

claims.text: Cooling must remove heat generated at chip, server, or rack level to maintain desired equipment temperatures and uninterrupted operation; cooling accounts for approximately 40% of total data center energy consumption.

support.text: Rong and colleagues are cited for the approximately 40% share.

citations.reference_entry: Rong H, Zhang H, Xiao S, Li C, Hu C. Optimizing energy consumption for data centers. Renew Sust Energ Rev. 2016;58:674-691. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2015.12.283.

claims.text: Air cooling is the traditional approach, while liquid cooling is becoming popular because of its high heat removal performance.

support.text: The distinction between air-cooled and liquid-cooled systems is introduced with a review citation.

citations.reference_entry: Khalaj AH, Halgamuge SK. A review on efficient thermal management of air- and liquid-cooled data centers: from chip to the cooling system. Appl Energy. 2017;205:1165-1188. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2017.08.037.

reading_path.meaning: The introduction develops the motivation announced in the Summary. Its perspective is operational and energy-focused: cooling is necessary infrastructure whose large energy share makes it a consequential target for improvement.

reading_path.location: Page 10454, Section 1, heat rejection and existing waste heat uses
reading_path.moves: Surveys established alternatives and identifies an earlier desalination proposal whose modeling details were absent.

claims.text: Both air-cooled and liquid-cooled data centers generally reject thermal energy to the environment through equipment such as dry towers or economizers.

support.text: Two reviews support this description of conventional heat rejection.

citations.reference_entry: Fulpagare Y, Bhargav A. Advances in data center thermal management. Renew Sust Energ Rev. 2015;43:981-996. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2014.11.056.
Ni J, Bai X. A review of air conditioning energy performance in data centers. Renew Sust Energ Rev. 2017;67:625-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2016.09.050.

claims.text: Data center heat can alternatively serve combined heating and cooling, district heating and hot water production, or vapor compression.

support.text: The authors supply one cited example for each application.

citations.reference_entry: Davies GF, Maidment GG, Tozer RM. Using data centres for combined heating and cooling: an investigation for London. Appl Therm Eng. 2016;94:296-304. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2015.09.111.

Oro E, Taddedo P, Salom J. Waste heat recovery from urban air cooled data centres to increase energy efficiency of district heating networks. Sust Cities Soc. 2019;45:522-542. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scs.2018.12.012.
Beitelmal AH, Patel CD. A steady-state model for the design and optimization of a centralized cooling system. Int J Energy Res. 2010;34:1239-1248. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.1663.

claims.text: Ebrahimi and colleagues proposed seawater desalination using data center waste heat or steam, but did not give modeling and performance assessment details.

support.text: The earlier proposal is located in a review of data center cooling and low-grade heat recovery.

citations.reference_entry: Ebrahimi K, Jones GF, Fleischer AS. A review of data center cooling technology, operating conditions and the corresponding low-grade waste heat recovery opportunities. Renew Sust Energ Rev. 2014;31:622-638. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2013.12.007.

reading_path.meaning: The discussion moves from the need to remove heat to the possibility of using it. The earlier desalination idea establishes a precedent while leaving room for the detailed assessment this article proposes.

reading_path.location: Page 10454, Section 1, desalination integration and energy-water framing
reading_path.moves: Reasons by analogy from other integrated energy systems, asserts practical potential, and gives the proposal a sustainable-development rationale.

claims.text: Desalination has been proposed in combination with nuclear power, marine energy and industry, solar energy, fuel cell and gas turbine systems, and thermoelectric coolers.

support.text: The authors cite the following integration studies as precedents.

citations.reference_entry: Khan SU, Danish SN, Haider S, Khan SU. Theoretical calculation simulation studies of ABV nuclear reactor coupled with desalination system. Int J Energy Res. 2015;39:1554-1563. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.3363.
Park S, Chun W, Kim N. Simulated production of electric power and desalination using solar-OTEC hybrid system. Int J Energy Res. 2017;41:637-649. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.3641.
Gude VG. Thermal desalination of ballast water using onboard waste heat in marine industry. Int J Energy Res. 2019;43:6026-6037. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.4647.
Shekarchi N, Shahnja F. A comprehensive review of solar-driven desalination technologies for off-grid greenhouses. Int J Energy Res. 2019;43:1357-1386. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.4268.
Leblanc J, Andrews J, Akbarzadeh A. Low-temperature solar-thermal multi-effect evaporation desalination systems. Int J Energy Res. 2010;34:393-403. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.1642.

Hosseini M, Dincer I, Ahmadi P, Avval HA, Ziaasharhagh M. Low-temperature solar-thermal multi-effect evaporation desalination systems. Int J Energy Res. 2013;37:426-434. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.1945.

Hosseini M, Dincer I, Ahmadi P, Avval HA, Ziaasharhagh M. Theoretical and experimental investigation of bubble column humidification and thermoelectric cooler dehumidification water desalination system. Int J Energy Res. 2020;44:890-901. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.4931.

claims.text: From those studies, the authors infer that low-temperature energy systems can be efficiently combined with desalination and that data center heat can supply sufficient energy for desalination units.

support.text: The preceding examples of desalination integration supply the analogy; no data center-specific calculation is presented at this point.

claims.text: Combining data center cooling and desalination is critically important because it addresses SDG 6, Clean Water and Sanitation, and SDG 7, Affordable and Clean Energy, and belongs within the energy-water nexus.

support.text: United Nations documents supply the policy frame.

citations.reference_entry: United Nations. Transforming our world: the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. 2015.
United Nations. Paris Agreement. 2015. https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/convention/application/pdf/english_paris_agreement.pdf. Accessed March 23, 2020)

claims.text: Detailed understanding of this combined concept is lacking, and system-scale waste heat utilization studies have largely concerned air-cooled rather than liquid-cooled data centers.

reading_path.meaning: The proposal now has both an engineering analogy and a policy rationale. The authors treat useful water production and efficient heat utilization as desirable together, then identify the absence of detailed liquid-cooling studies as a research gap.

reading_path.location: Pages 10454–10455, Section 1, direct liquid cooling and the authors' earlier work
reading_path.moves: Classifies cooling technologies, compares their advantages and drawbacks, and narrows the gap through prior experiments and modeling.

claims.text: Liquid cooling can remove higher heat flux than air cooling. Indirect liquid cooling is more established, but piping introduces leakage potential and its layout must be sized for the required cooling load.

Direct cooling uses dielectric liquids in contact with ICT surfaces, eliminating server- or rack-level liquid piping and allowing flexible adaptation to different loads. The authors identify jet impingement, spray cooling, and two-phase liquid immersion as direct methods.
Two-phase liquid immersion provides a more uniform equipment-surface temperature through latent heat transfer; direct methods may operate independently or alongside conventional air cooling.

support.text: The authors direct readers to four works for further details on liquid cooling.

citations.reference_entry: Saini M, Webb RL. Heat rejection limits of air cooled plane fin heat sinks for computer cooling. IEEE Trans Compon Packag Technol. 2013;26:71-79. https://doi.org/10.1109/TCAPT.2003.811465.

Tuma PE. Fluoroketone C2F5C(O)CF(CF3)2 as a heat transfer fluid for passive and pumped 2-phase applications. Paper presented at: Proceedings of the 24th Annual IEEE Semiconductor Thermal Measurement and Management Symposium (SEMI-THERM); March 16-20, 2008; San Jose (CA), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/STHERM.2008.4509386.

Tuma PE. The merits of open bath immersion cooling of datacom equipment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of the 26th Annual IEEE Semiconductor Thermal Measurement and Management Symposium (SEMI-THERM); February 21-25, 2010; Santa Clara (CA), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/STHERM.2010.5444305.
Bar-Cohen A, Arik M, Ohadi M. Direct liquid cooling of high flux micro and nano electronic components. Proc IEEE. 2006;94:1549-1570. https://doi.org/10.1109/JPROC.2006.879791.

claims.text: Despite work by Submer, GIGABYTE, 3M, and FUJITSU, system-scale thermal management and economic assessment of two-phase immersion remain insufficiently studied.

The authors previously obtained satisfactory steady performance in an experimental immersion system tested up to 21 kW, then modeled integration with a polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell to obtain low-carbon electricity at a cooling load near 6 kW.

support.text: The experimental and hybrid modeling studies provide the immediate research background.

citations.reference_entry: Wu C, Tong W, Kanbur BB, Duan F. Full-scale two-phase liquid immersion cooing data center system in tropical environment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of 2019 18th IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm); May 27-31, 2019; Las Vegas (NV), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/ITHERM.2019.8757316.

Kanbur BB, Wu C, Duan F. Combined heat and power generation via hybrid data center cooling-polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell system. Int J Energy Res. 2020;44:4759-4772. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.5256.

claims.text: Below 6 kW, waste heat utilization may be inefficient for low-carbon electricity generation or other familiar thermal processes, leaving a need for more efficient and economical low-load immersion systems.

reading_path.meaning: The broad research gap becomes a particular operating niche: low cooling loads. The earlier studies explain why these authors move from electricity generation toward another use for the available heat.

reading_path.location: Page 10455, Section 1, paragraph listing original contributions
reading_path.moves: States novelty claims, restates the proposed integration, and specifies the optimization objectives and design bounds.

claims.text: The authors claim that this particular hybrid has not previously been investigated and that it is the first use of two-phase liquid-immersion cooling waste heat for desalination.
The new exergy-cost matrix is presented as a potentially useful tool for future waste heat utilization studies of two-phase liquid-immersion systems.
The optimization seeks minimum distilled water cost and system product cost alongside maximum exergy efficiency, within the previously announced cooling-load and membrane-area bounds.

reading_path.meaning: The introduction closes by turning its gap into a declared contribution. The system concept and operating ranges repeat the Summary, while novelty and future methodological usefulness receive explicit emphasis.

reading_path.location: Page 10455, Section 2, seawater inlet and immersion tank operation
reading_path.moves: Describes the physical system, assigns stream identities, introduces site-specific inputs, and explains the phase-change mechanism.

claims.text: Stream 1 is seawater at 35 g/L salinity, 302.75 K, and 1 atm; the salinity represents standard seawater and the temperature represents Singapore seawater.

support.text: The salinity and temperature inputs are attributed to these sources.

citations.reference_entry: Al-Obaidani S, Curcio E, Macedonio F, Di Profio G, Al-Hinai H, Drioli E. Potential of membrane distillation in seawater desalination: thermal efficiency, sensitivity study and cost estimation. J Membr Sci. 2008;323:85-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2008.06.006.
World Sea Temperatures. Singapore sea temperatures. 2019. https://www.seatemperature.org/asia/singapore/singapore.htm. Accessed March 23, 2020.

claims.text: The system uses an assumed Euroflo EB120 pump and a customized immersion tank capable of handling up to 2 kW of server heat. The tank contains NOVEC 7100 dielectric liquid, whose boiling temperature is 61°C.
Constant server power is assumed so that steady-state thermodynamic assessments can be made.

support.text: The constant-power assumption is accompanied by a citation to Shah and Patel.

citations.reference_entry: Shah AJ, Patel CD. Designing environmentally sustainable electronic cooling systems using exergo-thermo-volumes. Int J Energy Res. 2009;33:1266-1277. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.1663.

claims.text: Server heat boils the dielectric bath. Rising vapor condenses on cooler pipes at the top of the tank and returns to the bath, while seawater flowing inside the pipes gains heat.

support.text: The authors refer back to their previously operated and verified immersion setup.

citations.reference_entry: Wu C, Tong W, Kanbur BB, Duan F. Full-scale two-phase liquid immersion cooing data center system in tropical environment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of 2019 18th IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm); May 27-31, 2019; Las Vegas (NV), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/ITHERM.2019.8757316.

reading_path.meaning: The proposed integration is now a physical sequence rather than an abstract combination. The local seawater conditions and equipment choices begin to define the particular system being modeled.

reading_path.location: Page 10455, Section 2, tank outlet and membrane distillation
reading_path.moves: Derives a temperature restriction, selects an engineering margin, and explains heat and mass transport through the membrane.

claims.text: Seawater leaving the tank cannot be hotter than the 61°C dielectric boiling temperature. The authors require an engineering temperature difference of 3 K below that boiling temperature.
Heated stream 3 enters the DCMD feed side. DCMD is described as the oldest membrane-distillation technique, with a membrane interface rather than an air gap or conductive-material interface.

support.text: The description of the membrane-distillation configuration cites Swaminathan and colleagues.

citations.reference_entry: Swaminathan J, Chung HW, Warsinger DM, Lienhard VJH. Membrane distillation model based on heat exchanger theory and configuration comparison. Appl Energy. 2016;184:491-505. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2016.09.090.

claims.text: Permeate-side inlet water begins as stream 5 at 293.15 K and becomes stream 6 after its circulation pump.

The temperature difference creates a vapor-pressure difference across a hydrophobic membrane that blocks liquid transport while permitting vapor transfer. Feed outlet stream 4 therefore has less mass flow than stream 3, while permeate outlet stream 7 has more than stream 6.

reading_path.meaning: The heat recovery pathway now reaches its product-forming mechanism. The 3 K margin is a selected design condition, while the changing stream flow rates follow from the described vapor transfer.

reading_path.location: Pages 10455–10456, Section 2, assumptions and input parameters
reading_path.moves: Makes simplifying assumptions explicit and fixes the hydraulic, membrane, and reference-state parameters.

claims.text: The model assumes steady-state operation, neglects membrane fouling, and treats the tank and DCMD module as having no heat loss.
The piping is also treated as insulated because the earlier experiment found very small pipe heat loss, attributed to insulation and a small fluid-to-ambient temperature difference.

support.text: The earlier experimental cooling study supplies the stated basis for this simplification.

citations.reference_entry: Wu C, Tong W, Kanbur BB, Duan F. Full-scale two-phase liquid immersion cooing data center system in tropical environment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of 2019 18th IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm); May 27-31, 2019; Las Vegas (NV), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/ITHERM.2019.8757316.

claims.text: Feed velocity is 1.85 m/s and permeate velocity is 2.92 m/s, with a hydraulic diameter of 0.003 m on both sides. Corrosion and salt deposition are neglected both in performance calculations and for pipeline damage.

The selected PVDF membrane has thickness 126 μm, thermal conductivity 0.41 W/mK, porosity 0.75, and pore size 0.22 μm. These membrane properties and the DCMD transfer characteristics come from Reference 31, which also serves as the validation source.

support.text: The input data are taken from the DCMD heat and mass transfer study by Termpiyakul and colleagues.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

claims.text: The thermodynamic reference state is 293.15 K and 1 atm.

reading_path.meaning: The model's scope is now explicit. The idealized treatment excludes fouling, corrosion, salt deposition, and external heat loss, while the membrane submodel is anchored to a particular published dataset.

reading_path.location: Page 10456, Section 3 opening and Figures 1–2
reading_path.moves: Organizes the modeling program and presents the physical and computational arrangements visually.

claims.text: The modeling comprises thermodynamic analysis, thermodynamic validation, economic analysis, thermoeconomic analysis, and multiobjective optimization.

Figure 1 shows seawater passing through a feed pump and the tank's condenser piping before entering the membrane feed channel; a separately pumped permeate stream passes along the other membrane side. The diagram also identifies the two pump power inputs.

Figure 2 shows a staged calculation: inlet properties and pump work lead to the heated feed state, iterative membrane calculations, mass transfer and outlet states, then energetic, exergetic, economic, and thermoeconomic assessments, ending with genetic-algorithm optimization.

reading_path.meaning: The figures consolidate the system description and make the dependencies among calculations visible. The article then begins following that computational sequence.

reading_path.location: Page 10457, Section 3.1, fluid properties and Equations (1)–(7)
reading_path.moves: Defines property correlations and derives stream enthalpy rates through pumps and the server tank.

claims.text: Water and seawater require different thermophysical correlations. The water enthalpy correlation uses Celsius temperature and yields J/kg; seawater enthalpy adds salinity-dependent terms, with coefficients deferred to Appendix A.

support.text: The property correlations are attributed to Sharqawy and colleagues. Equations (1)–(4) provide the water and seawater enthalpy and density relationships, with the seawater density coefficients deferred to Appendix B.

citations.reference_entry: Sharqawy MH, Lienhard VJH, Zubair SM. Thermophysical properties of seawater: a review of existing correlations and data. Desalin Water Treat. 2010;16:354-380. https://doi.org/10.5004/dwt.2010.1079.

claims.text: Mass flow is obtained from volumetric flow and density, with volumetric flow determined from hydraulic diameter and velocity. Multiplying mass flow by specific enthalpy gives the stream enthalpy rate.
Equations (5) and (6) add the respective pump power to the inlet enthalpy rates to obtain streams 2 and 6; Equation (7) adds server heat to stream 2 to obtain stream 3.
Because enthalpy depends on temperature, calculating stream 3 enthalpy allows its temperature to be found and supplies the feed temperature for the membrane model.

reading_path.meaning: The calculation begins with material properties and conservation of energy. This develops the earlier physical description into a procedure for obtaining the membrane's inlet conditions.

reading_path.location: Pages 10457–10458, Section 3.1, interfacial convection and Equations (8)–(11)
reading_path.moves: Divides the heat-transfer path into regions, defines temperatures, and selects a convection correlation.

claims.text: Heat passes from the warmer feed through the membrane to the cooler permeate, requiring separate expressions for feed-side convection, membrane transport, and permeate-side convection.

Equations (8) and (9) express the two convective heat fluxes as heat-transfer coefficients multiplied by bulk-to-membrane temperature differences. The specified temperature ordering is feed bulk, feed membrane surface, permeate membrane surface, then permeate bulk, from highest to lowest.

Equation (10) obtains the convective coefficient from Nusselt number, fluid thermal conductivity, and hydraulic diameter; Equation (11) supplies the Dittus and Boelter correlation using Reynolds number, Prandtl number, and a hydraulic-diameter-to-module-length term.

support.text: The selected convection correlation is cited to Reference 31.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

reading_path.meaning: The authors slow down at the membrane boundary layers. Bulk inlet temperatures alone are insufficient; the model must also obtain membrane-surface temperatures.

reading_path.location: Page 10458, Section 3.1, membrane heat and mass transfer, Equations (12)–(14)
reading_path.moves: Separates useful latent transport from conduction, defines mass flux, compares alternative calculations, and closes the local energy balance.

claims.text: Membrane heat transport has two mechanisms: latent heat associated with evaporation and conductive heat transfer. Equation (12) adds these contributions, using mass flux, vaporization enthalpy, membrane conductivity and thickness, and the membrane-surface temperature difference.

The study takes an experimental vaporization-enthalpy correlation from Reference 31; the authors also identify a physical derivation through nonequilibrium thermodynamics and the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.

support.text: Luo and Lior are cited for the alternative physical treatment and further modeling detail.

citations.reference_entry: Luo A, Lior N. Critical review of membrane distillation performance criteria. Desalin Water Treat. 2016;57:20093–20140. https://doi.org/10.1080/19443994.2016.1152637.

claims.text: Equation (13) defines mass flux from the feed's mass-flow decrease, or equivalently the permeate's increase, divided by membrane area. The authors regard this as easier for experimental setups than methods requiring permeability or detailed membrane-characterization inputs.

Alternative flux calculations use membrane permeability and vapor-pressure difference or nonequilibrium thermodynamic and membrane parameters; experimental characterization of those parameters can introduce additional uncertainty.

support.text: The uncertainty point is accompanied by a membrane-characterization study.

citations.reference_entry: Tanis Kanbur MB, Peinador RI, Hu X, Calvo JI, Chew JW. Membrane characterization via evapoporometry (EP) and liquid-liquid displacement porosimetry (LLDP) techniques. J Membr Sci. 2019;586:248-258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2019.05.077.

claims.text: With external module heat loss neglected, Equation (14) sets feed-side, membrane, and permeate-side heat fluxes equal.

reading_path.meaning: The membrane model now distinguishes heat that accompanies vapor production from heat conducted across the membrane. Equality of the regional fluxes supplies the condition needed to solve the unknown surface temperatures.

reading_path.location: Page 10458, Section 3.1, iterative solution, outlet states, and Equations (15)–(17)
reading_path.moves: Explains the numerical procedure, qualifies a small-scale approximation, and extends the calculation to outlet enthalpy and entropy.

claims.text: The model estimates the feed-side membrane temperature and iterates Equations (8)–(14) until their heat fluxes agree, after which mass flux, transferred mass, and temperatures can be obtained.
Prandtl numbers are calculated separately for the two sides using the mean of each bulk and membrane-surface temperature.

support.text: The temperature-averaging procedure follows Reference 31.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

claims.text: A mean-temperature approximation is reasonable for small DCMD setups, but must be replaced by dynamic observation of temperature gradients for large commercial systems because those gradients may be nonlinear.

Equation (15) equates feed enthalpy loss and permeate enthalpy gain to heat flux multiplied by membrane area, allowing outlet states to be calculated. Equations (16) and (17) then give separate water and seawater entropy correlations, with seawater coefficients supplied in Appendix C.

support.text: The entropy correlations use the same seawater-property reference as the enthalpy correlations.

citations.reference_entry: Sharqawy MH, Lienhard VJH, Zubair SM. Thermophysical properties of seawater: a review of existing correlations and data. Desalin Water Treat. 2010;16:354-380. https://doi.org/10.5004/dwt.2010.1079.

reading_path.meaning: The local heat-transfer model becomes a complete stream-state calculation. The explicit scale qualification limits how directly its averaging procedure can be carried into a commercial installation.

reading_path.location: Pages 10458–10459, Section 3.1, exergy formulation and Equations (18)–(19)
reading_path.moves: Introduces second-law accounting, defines a reference-state measure, and states exclusions and balance terms.

claims.text: Exergy analysis supplies destruction and loss information that energy analysis cannot provide.

Equation (18) defines stream specific exergy as its enthalpy difference from the reference state minus reference temperature multiplied by its entropy difference; multiplication by mass flow gives exergy rate.

support.text: The equation is introduced with an earlier exergy-analysis paper.

citations.reference_entry: Kanbur BB, Xiang L, Dubey S, Choo FH, Duan F. A micro cogeneration system with LNG cold utilization-part 2: exergy analyses. Energy Procedia. 2017;105:1910-1917. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.egypro.2017.03.559.

claims.text: Chemical exergy is omitted because, the authors state, there is no change in the streams' chemical components.

Equation (19) balances fuel exergy against product, destruction, loss, and gain terms. Heat-loss exergy is neglected under the zero-heat-loss assumption, while the gain term must be retained because the servers supply heat.

support.text: The discussion directs readers to two general thermodynamic references for further exergy detail.

citations.reference_entry: Bejan A, Tsatsaronis G, Moran MJ. Thermal Design and Optimization. New York: Wiley; 1996.
Cengel YA, Boles MA. Thermodynamics: an Engineering Approach. 5th ed. Boston, MA: McGraw-Hill; 2006.

reading_path.meaning: The analysis adds a second-law perspective to the already established energy balances. The treatment remains tied to the earlier idealization of an insulated system and explicitly excludes chemical exergy.

reading_path.location: Page 10459, Section 3.1, performance criteria and Equations (20)–(25)
reading_path.moves: Defines assessment metrics and connects exergy accounting to a sustainability indicator.

claims.text: Equation (20) defines cooling COP as server heat removal divided by feed-pump power. Equation (21) defines membrane thermal efficiency as latent heat flux divided by total heat flux.
GOR measures vapor-associated heat transfer relative to total heat input, and higher GOR is desired. PR measures clean water production relative to inlet feed flow.

support.text: Equations (22) and (23) express these definitions using latent heat transport, server heat, product mass flow, and inlet feed mass flow.

claims.text: The authors identify exergy efficiency as a principal exergetic criterion. Equation (24), labeled as exergy efficiency, prints the same latent-heat-output-to-server-heat expression that appears for GOR in Equation (22).

The sustainability index is fuel exergy divided by exergy destruction. The authors state that increasing fuel exergy through better utilization, or decreasing destruction through better design, increases this index.

support.text: The index is attributed to Rosen and colleagues and expressed in Equation (25).

citations.reference_entry: Rosen MA, Dincer I, Kanoglu M. Role of exergy in increasing efficiency and sustainability and reducing environmental impact. Energ Policy. 2008;36:128-137. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2007.09.006.

reading_path.meaning: The article establishes the vocabulary through which it will report performance. The printed expressions are recorded as they stand, without replacing them with inferred alternatives.

reading_path.location: Pages 10459–10460, Section 3.2, DCMD model validation; Table 1 on page 10461
reading_path.moves: Compares the membrane submodel with an existing study, quantifies agreement, and draws a validation conclusion.
